titles.511: Annotatio IV §.VI open: Second century — Ignatius, Justin, Irenaeus on the true Eucharistic sentence
titles.512: Annotatio IV §.VI: Ignatius to Smyrna — Eucharist is the Savior’s flesh; Theodoret still cites it
titles.513: Annotatio IV §.VI: Justin Martyr — Eucharistic bread remains after consecration; Cosinus epiphonema
titles.514: Annotatio IV §.VI: Irenaeus — Eucharist of two things, terrestrial and celestial (observations 1–2)
titles.515: Annotatio IV §.VI cont.: Irenaeus (3–4) — two things of the Eucharist; celestial = supernatural presence mode

latin.511: §. VI. Itaque SECULO Apostolicum proximè excipiente, i. e. Christianæ æræ SECUNDO, dictam de Eucharistia sententiam veram à Christo & Apostolis sibi traditam, apertè satis professi sunt Martyres Christi præstantissimi, IGNATIUS Antiochenus, Seculi hujus initiô; JUSTINUS MARTYR medio, nec non IRENÆUS, sub finem ejusdem celebres, ita verò veritatem Eucharisticam professi, ut primus ad præcipuam Eucharistiæ partem, fide sola tenendam; secundus, ne pars hæc adesse sola crederetur, ad minus principalem, in præcipuam neutiquam transmutandam; Tertius denique, ad utramque, nec non ad utriusq; cùm præsentiam ac participationem, tùm præsentiæ & participationis modum, & suæ, & nostrum omnium, Mentis oculos conversos voluerit.
latin.512: IGNATII verba leguntur in Epistola ad Smyrenses, quibus affirmat: Eucharistiam esse Carnem Servatoris nostri Jesu Christi, quæ pro peccatis nostris passa est, quam Pater suâ benignitate suscitavit. Quæ verba proptereà fidei sublestæ neutiquam censenda, nec miserè interpolatis Ignatii superstitibus Scriptis adhuc, accensenda, quod illa etiam Seculo Vtô Theodoretus commemorat, Dialogo tertio apathēs seu impatibilis ditô.
latin.513: JUSTINUS MARTYR panem Eucharisticum, etiam post consecrationem, eundem permanere, inque alimoniam carnis nostræ (etsi vulgaris amplius non sit, utpote fidelibus communionem corporis Christi tributurus) edocere annisus, in Apol. 2. ad Antoninum Imperatorem prope finem, ita disserit: Postquam Præses gratias egit & acclamavit populus, illi qui à nobis dicuntur Diaconi, seu Ministri, dant cuique præsentium, quod sumant de pane & vino: Et hoc alimentum à nobis vocatur Eucharistia; Non enim ut vulgarem panem, neque ut vulgare poculum hæc sumimus: Sed quemadmodum per verbum Dei, Caro factus Jesus Christus Servator noster, carnem & sanguinem pro salute nostra habuit, sic etiam per verbum precationis & gratiarum actionis, sacratam ab ipso alimoniam, QUÆ MUTATA NUTRIT NOSTRAS CARNES ET SANGUINEM, illius incarnati Jesu carnem & sanguinem esse didicimus. Ad hoc respiciens Cosinus Episcopus Dunelmensis, adductis à se quoque Justini verbis sequens epiphonema annexit: Quare, inquit, & substantia panis etiam post Consecrationem manet & verè corruptibilis cibus est, quod de Christi corpore immortali dici non potest: Neque enim caro Christi carnem nostram alit, nec in eam mutatur, sed cibus iste, qui sacramentaliter Caro Christi dicitur. Caro autem Christi nutrit ad vitam æternam. cit. loc. p. 58.
latin.514: IRENÆUS tandem uti prolixius ac crebrius, ita & plenius distinctiusve, rem veritatemque Eucharisticam persequitur. Primò quidem, Librô contra Hæreses quarto cap. 34. ex duabus rebus S. Eucharistiam constare disertissimè ratus: Panis, inquit, qui est à terra, percipiens invocationem Dei, jam non communis panis est, sed Eucharistia, duabus rebus constans, terrena & cælestis. Ubi observes velim, divum Martyrem (1) Panem post consecrationem factam, non amplius communem, sed ab omni communi usu sejunctum, interim tamen adhuc panem salutare. (2) Panem hunc ab omni communi usu separatum, non dicere ipsum corpus Christi, quasi in hoc transmutatum, sed verò Eucharistiam, i. e. panem, Eucharistiæ S. destinatum consecratumque.
latin.515: (3) Eucharistiam S., non verò panem, ex duabus rebus censere constare, ne quis cum pane, etiam extra usum Eucharistiæ legitimum, corpus Christi conjungi arbitretur. (4) Duarum rerum alteram, terrenam vocitare, scil. panem è terra natum, alteram verò cælestem, eòque non corpus Christi naturaliter seu corporaliter præsens, quod ipsum corpus res cælestis, non nisi per Hæresin Manichaicam, juxta Spiritûs S. verò mentem, res omnino terrena haberi debet, ex Massa Mariæ sanguinea formata, in utero ejusdem concepta, fota, nutrita, definitô tempore, ex utero materno in mundi lucem egressa, nobis & nostris Infantibus per omnia, etiam ratione præsentiæ localis, unico exceptô peccatô, simillima, Sed verò ob cœlestem unicè ac supernaturalem in Eucharistia præsentiæ modum, cælestis dicta, animarum nostrarum fidelium, eatenus ex cœlo, quin ex Spiritu S. natarum, genuinum pabulum, etiam in corporibus fidelium, saluberrimum usum olim habiturum, i. e. horum beatam ad vitam æternam, procuraturum resurrectionem.
latin.516: Ita enim iterum Irenæus Lib. 5. contra Hæret. cap. 12. pergit: Quemadmodum granum tritici, decidens in terram & dissolutum, multiplex surgit, & percipiens verbum Dei fit Eucharistia; (quod est corpus & sanguis Christi); Sic & nostra, scil. fidelium, corpora, ex eo nutrita, & reposita in terram ac resoluta, resurgent (scil. cum gaudio) in suo tempore. Quin, ne quis sibi imaginetur, sanctissimum Patrem opinari, corpora nostra corpore Christi nutriri, non verò pane Eucharistico potius ab omni usu communi sejuncto, addit paulò post: Per Creaturam nutrimur, Creaturam autem ipse nobis præstat; Cùm Calicem, qui est creatura, suum sanguinem, & eum panem, qui est creatura, suum Corpus confirmavit. Quando ergo Calix & panis percipiunt verbum Dei, fit Eucharistia sanguinis & corporis Christi (non ipse sanguis & corpus Christi) ex quibus (calice scil. & pane) augetur & consistit carnis nostræ substantia. Quandoquidem non sine magna absurditate impietateque diceretur, ex naturali Christi corpore & sanguine, nostra corpora augeri ac consistere; cùm nihil corpus nostrum naturaliter augere possit, nisi quod per alterationem in carnem nostram & sanguinem convertitur, quod de corpore Christi incorruptibili affirmare blasphemum est.

pass_a.511: §. VI. Therefore in the age next receiving the Apostolic, i.e. the SECOND of the Christian era, the most excellent Martyrs of Christ openly enough professed the said true sentence concerning the Eucharist handed to them by Christ and the Apostles — IGNATIUS of Antioch at the beginning of this age; JUSTIN MARTYR in the middle; and also IRENÆUS, famous toward its end — professing Eucharistic truth so that the first turned the mind’s eyes to the chief part of the Eucharist to be held by faith alone; the second, lest that part be believed to be present alone, to the less principal, by no means to be transmuted into the chief; the Third finally to both, and to both presence and participation and the mode of presence and participation, of his own and of us all.
pass_a.512: IGNATIUS’s words are read in the Epistle to the Smyrnaeans, by which he affirms: that the Eucharist is the Flesh of our Savior Jesus Christ, which suffered for our sins, which the Father by His kindness raised. Which words are therefore by no means to be judged of weakened faith, nor still counted among Ignatius’s wretchedly interpolated surviving Writings, because Theodoret also in the fifth century commemorates them in the third Dialogue titled apathēs or Impassible.
pass_a.513: JUSTIN MARTYR, having endeavored to teach that the Eucharistic bread, even after consecration, remains the same and goes into the nourishment of our flesh (though it is no longer common, as about to give the faithful communion of Christ’s body), near the end of Apol. 2 to Emperor Antoninus discourses thus …: this food is called by us Eucharist; for we do not take these as common bread or a common cup … we have learned that the food consecrated by the word of prayer and thanksgiving, WHICH CHANGED NOURISHES OUR FLESHES AND BLOOD, is the flesh and blood of that incarnate Jesus. Looking to this, Cosinus Bishop of Durham, having also brought Justin’s words, annexed this epiphonema: Wherefore, he says, the substance of bread also remains after Consecration and is truly corruptible food, which cannot be said of Christ’s immortal body: For neither does Christ’s flesh nourish our flesh, nor is it changed into it, but this food which is sacramentally called the Flesh of Christ. But Christ’s Flesh nourishes unto eternal life. cit. loc. p. 58.
pass_a.514: IRENÆUS at last pursues the Eucharistic matter and truth both more fully and more distinctly as he does more at length and more often. First indeed, in Book 4 against Heresies ch. 34, judging most expressly that the Sacred Eucharist consists of two things: The bread, he says, which is from the earth, receiving the invocation of God, is now no longer common bread, but Eucharist, consisting of two things, earthly and heavenly. Where I would have you observe the holy Martyr (1) still greeting as bread the bread after consecration done — no longer common, but severed from every common use. (2) saying this bread separated from every common use is not itself Christ’s body as if transmuted into this, but truly the Eucharist, i.e. bread destined and consecrated for the Sacred Eucharist.
pass_a.515: (3) judging that the Sacred Eucharist, not the bread, consists of two things, lest anyone think Christ’s body is joined with the bread even outside the lawful use of the Eucharist. (4) calling one of the two things earthly, namely bread born from the earth, but the other heavenly — and thus not Christ’s body naturally or corporally present, which body itself as a heavenly thing, unless by Manichaean Heresy, according to the Holy Spirit’s true mind ought to be held an entirely earthly thing, formed from Mary’s bloody mass … most like us and our Infants in all things even as to local presence, sin alone excepted — But called heavenly on account of the solely heavenly and supernatural mode of presence in the Eucharist, genuine food of our faithful souls born from heaven, nay from the Holy Spirit, hereafter to have most wholesome use even in the bodies of the faithful, i.e. to procure their blessed resurrection unto eternal life.
pass_a.516: For so again Irenæus proceeds in Book 5 against Heresies ch. 12: As a grain of wheat, falling into the earth and dissolved, rises manifold, and receiving the word of God becomes Eucharist (which is the body and blood of Christ); so also our bodies, namely of the faithful, nourished from it and laid in the earth and dissolved, shall rise (namely with joy) in their time. Nay, lest anyone imagine the most holy Father thinks our bodies are nourished by Christ’s body rather than by Eucharistic bread severed from every common use, he adds a little later: We are nourished by the Creature, and He Himself supplies us the Creature; Since He confirmed the Cup, which is a creature, as His blood, and that bread, which is a creature, as His Body. When therefore the Cup and bread receive the word of God, there is made the Eucharist of the blood and body of Christ (not the blood and body of Christ themselves) from which (cup and bread) the substance of our flesh is increased and consists. Seeing it would be said not without great absurdity and impiety that our bodies are increased and consist from Christ’s natural body and blood; since nothing can naturally increase our body except what is converted by alteration into our flesh and blood, which it is blasphemous to affirm of Christ’s incorruptible body.

511: §.VI: in the SECOND Christian age after the Apostolic, the leading martyrs openly professed the true Eucharistic sentence from Christ and the Apostles.

Ignatius (start) turns the mind to the chief part held by faith alone; Justin (middle) to the lesser part not to be turned into the chief; Irenaeus (end) to both — presence, participation, and their mode.
512: Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans: the Eucharist is the Flesh of our Savior Jesus Christ, which suffered for our sins and which the Father raised.
Not to be written off as weak faith or among interpolated Ignatian writings — Theodoret in the fifth century still cites them in Dialogue 3 (apathēs / Impassible).
513: Justin (Apol. 2): after consecration the Eucharistic bread remains the same and feeds our flesh — no longer common, yet the food ‘changed’ that nourishes our flesh and blood we have learned is the flesh and blood of the incarnate Jesus.

Cosinus of Durham: therefore bread-substance remains after consecration as truly corruptible food — Christ’s immortal body does not nourish or change into our flesh; this food is sacramentally called Christ’s Flesh, which nourishes unto eternal life.
514: Irenaeus (Adv. Haer. 4.34) more fully: the Sacred Eucharist consists of two things — earthly and heavenly. Bread from earth receiving God’s invocation is no longer common bread but Eucharist.

(1) After consecration it is still bread, only severed from common use. (2) That separated bread is not itself Christ’s body as if transmuted — it is Eucharist: bread destined and consecrated for the sacrament.
515: (3) The two things belong to the Eucharist, not to the bread alone — lest Christ’s body be joined to bread even outside lawful use. (4) Earthly = bread from earth; heavenly is not Christ’s body naturally/corporally present (that body is an earthly thing from Mary’s mass, like us except sin).
It is called heavenly for the solely supernatural presence-mode in the Eucharist — genuine food of faithful souls from the Spirit, someday serving even their bodies toward blessed resurrection.
516: Irenaeus Adv. Haer. 5.12: as wheat falls, dissolves, and rises manifold into Eucharist (body and blood of Christ), so faithful bodies nourished from it shall rise. We are nourished by the Creature He supplies — cup and bread as creature confirmed as His blood and Body.

When cup and bread receive God’s word there is made the Eucharist of His blood and body — not the blood and body themselves — from which our flesh’s substance increases. To say our bodies grow from Christ’s natural incorruptible body would be absurd and blasphemous.
